title: Motion-Aligned Word Embeddings for Text-to-Motion Generation
one_liner: The paper repairs a weak link in text-to-motion systems by changing word embeddings so motion words carry information that lines up with real body movement segments.
lead: Text-to-motion models generate human pose sequences from language prompts. They often borrow text encoders from large language models trained on generic text, then expect those encoders to understand fine motion detail such as turning direction, speed, limb usage, and temporal order. That expectation is too strong. Generic language training teaches broad semantics, but it does not explicitly bind words such as clockwise, crouch, or quickly to skeletal movement patterns. This paper focuses on that mismatch at the word embedding level. A word embedding is the learned vector, meaning list of numbers, used to represent a word before later layers process it. The authors introduce Motion-Aligned Text Encoding, or MATE, which injects motion-specific supervision into those word representations. It does this with localized text-to-motion alignment and with a disentanglement module that tries to isolate the motion meaning associated with each word instead of mixing many motion factors together.

problem.h2: Generic text encoders blur motion semantics
paras: A text-to-motion system must translate a sentence into a sequence of body poses over time. Some parts of the sentence refer to actions, some to direction, some to speed, and some to body parts. If the text encoder represents these words only in generic linguistic terms, downstream motion generation has to infer the detailed kinematic effect later, often from weak supervision.

The mismatch is strongest for words whose meaning depends on movement itself. Directional adverbs, tempo words, and body-specific verbs should map to distinct motion patterns, but pretrained language encoders may place them near other words based on text co-occurrence rather than on physical movement. The paper argues that this misalignment starts early, inside the word representation, so it should be corrected there instead of only in later fusion layers.

callout.html: Text-to-motion models inherit word representations that were not trained to distinguish fine-grained movement semantics, so prompts and generated motion drift apart.

panels.title: 1. Prompt contains motion-specific words
panels.caption: The prompt specifies direction and speed, not just a coarse action category.

panels.title: 2. Generic encoder mixes meanings
panels.caption: The word representations capture language regularities but not enough motion detail.

panels.title: 3. Localize words to motion segments
panels.caption: Sub-phrases attend to the parts of the motion sequence where their effect appears.

panels.title: 4. Separate word-specific motion cues
panels.caption: Contrastive prototypes push the representation of each motion word toward its own kinematic signature.

panels.title: 5. Generator follows the prompt more closely
panels.caption: The edited word representations supply cleaner control signals to the motion generator.

steps.text: Start from a pretrained language model and obtain word-level representations for the prompt.
Estimate which sub-text aligns with which segment of the motion sequence using soft attention, which means weighted focus rather than a single hard boundary.

Create representative kinematic patterns for different motion words so the model has explicit targets for directional and temporal semantics, because each word can then be compared against a motion pattern that isolates its intended body change.
Use contrastive training, which means pulling matched word-motion pairs together and pushing mismatched ones apart, to separate the motion meaning tied to each word.

steps.b: Plug the edited encoder into existing generators
steps.text: Feed the motion-aligned text representations into standard text-to-motion pipelines with only small integration changes.

paras: The paper changes the text representation that conditions motion generation. Instead of leaving the language model's word vectors untouched, it adds motion supervision directly to them through localization and contrastive kinematic prototypes.

hidden.name: word-to-motion specificity
paras: The hidden quantity is how much of a motion sequence can be attributed to a specific word or phrase. In many datasets, several movement factors are active at once: action type, direction, speed, limb emphasis, and timing. If all of those factors stay entangled, a model cannot tell whether quickly should change tempo, whether clockwise should change turn direction, or whether both words should alter the same segment.

MATE tries to increase specificity. Localization narrows where in time a word should matter. The prototype-based contrastive objective narrows what kind of body motion that word should correspond to. Together, those constraints give the generator a cleaner conditioning signal because the representation for a motion word carries a more distinct kinematic meaning.

heat.caption: The important cells isolate which words should control which parts of the motion sequence.

reads.html: The model should know exactly which part of the movement each motion word is responsible for.
Word representations need localized and disentangled kinematic grounding so distinct motion semantics do not collapse into one mixed sentence feature.

mechanism.h2: Why editing the word representation helps
paras: The method works because the conditioning error starts before motion generation. If the text encoder already confuses directional, temporal, and action semantics, later layers receive a blended signal and must guess which movement property each word should control. Correcting only the generator leaves that upstream ambiguity in place.

Localization supplies temporal structure. It tells the model where a phrase should apply in the motion sequence, so the representation for bend down is tied to a different span from the representation for stand up. Disentanglement supplies semantic structure. It pushes the representation for clockwise toward motion examples with the matching rotation pattern and away from opposite or unrelated patterns.

These two constraints make the prompt representation more usable for any downstream text-to-motion model because the generator now receives word features whose motion meaning is less mixed and more directly tied to observable body movement.

math.words: Matched word-motion pairs are trained to score higher than mismatched pairs so each motion word acquires a more distinct kinematic identity.
math.equation: alignment loss = positive pair score minus negative pair score, optimized so matched pairs rank above mismatched pairs
symbols: a motion word and a motion segment that belong together
a motion word paired with an unrelated or opposite motion segment
how well the text representation matches the kinematic prototype
training objective that separates correct from incorrect matches

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the prompt contains the word clockwise.
A localized motion segment shows the body rotating to the right over several frames.
That segment forms the positive pair for clockwise.
A leftward rotation segment forms a negative pair.
Training increases the score of clockwise with the rightward segment and decreases the score with the leftward segment, so the word vector carries direction-specific motion information.

math.note: The objective is useful only when localization is reasonably good, because the contrastive step needs plausible candidate segments to know what each word should align with.

charts.title: Generic text encoder
charts.note: A generic encoder is easy to plug in, but it gives weak control over fine movement semantics because the word vectors were not trained on kinematic alignment.

charts.title: MATE-enhanced encoder
charts.note: Localization and prototype-based alignment raise specificity while keeping the encoder usable inside existing text-to-motion systems.

items.html: If the model aligns a word to the wrong time span, the prototype objective reinforces the wrong movement evidence and corrupts the word representation.
Some phrases jointly express action, speed, and direction, so a simple word-level split may not fully separate which factor caused which body change.

items.b: Benchmark motion data may be narrow.
items.html: If the training motions cover limited body types or action styles, the learned prototypes can become too specific to those datasets and generalize poorly.
Check whether aligned spans are plausible, include negative examples that truly differ in movement meaning, and test the edited encoder across several motion generators instead of only one.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a demo with prompts that differ by one motion word at a time, such as left versus right, slowly versus quickly, or bend versus stretch. Show the generated pose sequence and highlight the motion spans that the model aligns to each phrase.

The demo should confirm that changing one motion word changes the expected body behavior while leaving unrelated parts of the sequence relatively stable. It should also show that the MATE-enhanced encoder creates sharper differences than a generic text encoder on the same generator.
demo.closing: A strong demo makes the paper's point visible at the word level: the gain comes from giving motion words their own kinematic meaning instead of letting that meaning stay buried in a generic sentence representation.
